2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: By defying the Supreme Court’s one-time direction to also light the ceremonial Karthigai Deepam at a stone pillar , claimed by Hindu groups to be a Deepathoon, atop the Thirupparankundram hills, the Tamil Nadu government has disregarded a constitutional body’s authority. Believed to be Lord Murugan’s first abode, the hills have, for centuries , witnessed an intersection of religious faiths, with occasional skirmishes leading to tense flare-ups and legal battles. They house the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy, Uchchi Pillaiyar and Kashi Viswanathar temples; Sultan Sikkandar Avulia Dargah; and also Jain beds. Historically, the lamp is lit near the Pillaiyar temple. In 1994-95, the Hindu Munnani precipitated matters, claiming that the moksha deepam (for departed souls) and Karthigai Deepam were being lit at the same place. It demanded the lamp be lit at a pillar, 50 metres from the Dargah. In multiple legal battles, successive governments, backed by hereditary priests (Sthaneeka Bhattars) , opposed the demand. Even in 1862 and 1912, courts had disallowed lamp lighting near the Dargah. The BJP and its affiliates have, since, aggressively weaponised the demand in the name of Hindu religious rights. Against this backdrop, last year, the Madras High Cour t’s Madurai Bench, relying on the 1931 Privy Council ruling on ownership of the hills, held that “for the sake of protecting its property, the [Subramania Swamy] temple management is obliged to light the festival lamp at the Deepathoon” . The DMK government defied the order. Later, a Division Bench upheld the verdict. While staying this order recently, the Supreme Court cited the festival’s proximity to permit the lamp to be lit at the Deepathoon this year alone , clarifying that this did not constitute “essential religious practice”. The State filed a review petition , arguing when no right is recognised prima facie, a direction altering the existing position lacks judicial foundation. On Karthigai Deepam day, November 24, with the review pending, the government walked a tightrope. The Collector assured the High Court of compliance. Yet, the lamp was lit only at the traditional spot . The Collector has now apologised to the Court, blaming the temple’s Board of Trustees for not authorising the proposed lighting team at the Deepathoon. The administration has thus attempted to distinguish its proclaimed intent to comply with judicial directions from customs governed by the trustees. But it remains exposed to the charge of colluding with the temple authorities to breach a judicial mandate. The Deepathoon may be a mischievous prop deployed by self-serving Hindu groups, but the pillar stands on temple property. The State could have permitted the limited lighting, leaving the onus on the Court, without endorsing the Deepathoon claim or compromising religious amity. A democracy can remain healthy only when its constitutional pillars do not collide with one another.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: court / Tamil Nadu / religion and belief / history / Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam / democracy / customs and tradition / constitution

1. Core Context & Background: The new U.S. tariffs must not erode India’s stand on a trade deal

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The latest U.S. tariffs on India are nothing more than a pressure tactic to push for the signing of a trade deal. The U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed to levy a tariff of 25% for India’s apparent use of strategic excess manufacturing capacity to the detriment of American industry. This is the second-highest tariff rate the USTR has applied across the 14 countries that it has taken action against. The pressure on India does not come from the 25% rate but from the 17% this could be reduced to if it signs a trade deal with the U.S. This latest action is yet another example of how, despite the frothiness of India-U.S. trade relations over the past year and a half, the actual substance has not changed. The 25% rate now proposed, which is net of existing tariffs, is nearly the same as the 26% rate that U.S. President Donald Trump had first announced when he unveiled his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariffs in April 2025. Indeed, it is exactly the same as the 25% tariff he finally imposed in July 2025, before he imposed an additional 25% for India’s Russian oil imports. The 17% rate is also only marginally lower than the 18% that the two countries had agreed on in their joint statement in February 2026. It is also just one percentage point lower than the tariffs on competitors such as Indonesia and Malaysia. The allegation of India having excess capacity does not hold water. Indeed, were India to have excess manufacturing capacity in any sector, it would be the Government of India that would be the first to announce it with great fanfare, instead of denying it as it did. After all, that has been its aim since 2014. Yet, even a basic assessment of India’s import dependence and the fact that manufacturing’s share in GDP is lower now than a decade ago shows that India is far from having excess manufacturing capacity in any sector. Further, higher tariffs are unlikely to reduce America’s imports of the goods from India that it does depend on. The USTR mentioned generic pharmaceuticals, telecommunication equipment, and renewable energy goods. The first two are items that India has developed expertise in, which is distinct from strategic excess capacity. A relatively small tariff disadvantage will not substantially erode the attractiveness of these Indian products. Renewable energy imports from India have swelled because the U.S. is reducing its purchases from China. Hanging over all of this are the 100% tariffs related to the purchase of Russian oil, which have only temporarily been paused. India has so far held off on signing a deal, and must go ahead with one only if it is convinced that the benefits at least equal the costs.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: USA / India / taxes and duties / manufacturing and engineering / industrial production / trade policy / Russia / oil and gas - upstream activities / Indonesia / Malaysia / imports / pharmaceutical / telecommunication equipment / renewable energy / China

The Chennai Grandmaster was in considerable time trouble on multiple occasions, but managed to solve his problems and found proper answers to the questions posed to him on the board by the confident Sindarov. The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival. Sindarov is just six months older than Gukesh, making the Geneva match the youngest in the 140-year-old history of the World championship: both players are 20. It is remarkable that Gukesh has already seen the highs and lows of life at such a young age. For his opponent, the last one year has been better than a dream: from World No. 26 he has risen to No. 4. Chess is getting younger. The next World championship could also very well have two young contenders. Grandmasters are usually said to peak when they are around 30 and chess is one game that even older players have continued to excel in. Viswanathan Anand was 48 when he won the World rapid chess championship . The match between Gukesh and Sindarov has attracted considerable interest from across the sporting world. After the 1972 match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer — the defining moment of world chess — the World championship has earned a reputation as one of the planet’s most important sporting events. No battle between two of the world’s most talented men in chess has ever disappointed.

1. Core Context & Background: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance. The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: political parties / Bharatiya Janata Party / Punjab / voting / Indian National Congress / General Elections 2024 / Shiromani Akali Dal / Aam Aadmi Party / agriculture / economy / welfare

Following a brief inspection of the temple precincts, the former judges chaired a consultative meeting with the temple priests (bhattars), senior Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) officials, District Collector Nishant Krishna and senior officials of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF). During the closed-door deliberations, the judicial delegation sought detailed briefings from the bhattars regarding traditional rituals and customary practices associated with the shrine and the hilltop. Temple administrators and the District Collector apprised the judges of the logistical measures currently in place to regulate crowd movement and maintain public order. The judges emphasised the need for strict adherence to established legal frameworks while ensuring that routine religious observances continued without disruption. Following the judicial review, personnel from the CRPF formally took over security responsibilities at the foothills and around the contested Deepathoon site. Amidst the developments, a group of devotees and members of Hindu outfits attempted to breach police barricades to ascend the hill towards the Deepathoon pillar. Armed CRPF contingents have since established a multi-tiered security cordon along the trekking paths and entry points leading up the hillock, working in coordination with the local police and district administration. Essential items such as oil, a lamp and other materials were taken to the deepathoon site.

It is revered as Pampa Matha, and the river is associated with the concept of motherhood. It is the duty of every devotee of Lord Ayyappa to keep the river clean,” he said.
